item.title: A programmable quantum photonic platform integrating coherent emitters
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Monolithic GaAs circuit simultaneously operates two individually tunable p-i-n InAs quantum dots and a cryogenic NEMS optical router, achieving g(2)(0)=(0.62±0.07)% and raw two-photon interference visibility of VHOM=(62.2±6.7)%.

Grade 0.465 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Hanna Salamon, Mikkel T. Mikkelsen, Zhe Liu, Peter Lodahl, Severin Krüger, Arne Ludwig, Leonardo Midolo

Figure

(a) Resonance fluorescence spectrum (linewidth ΓRF=351.8±28.0 MHz) and decay rate (̳γ= 1.55±0.08ns⁻¹). (c) Two-photon interference correlation counts versus time delay showing VHOM=(62.2±6.7)% across parallel and perpendicular polarizations at a 50:50 NEMS router setting.

Asks

Can coherent, individually tunable quantum-dot emitters be monolithically integrated with programmable, cryogenic-compatible photonic routing elements on a single chip?

But

Measurements performed at approximately 5 K in a closed-cycle cryostat. Laser leakage and finite frequency scan steps degraded resonance fluorescence HOM visibility and scattering extinction.

Tools

GaAs p-i-n membrane platform · InAs self-assembled quantum dots · NEMS directional coupler router · Photonic crystal waveguides · Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs)

Abstract

Photonic quantum technologies require the integration of high-quality quantum light sources with programmable photonic circuitry to enable on-chip quantum information processing. Semiconductor quantum dots have emerged as a leading platform for quantum light generation, yet their monolithic integration with cryogenic-compatible, programmable photonic circuitry remains challenging. Here we demonstrate a programmable quantum photonic platform that enables simultaneous control of highly coherent quantum dot-based single photon emitters and reconfigurable optical elements at cryogenic temperatures. System-level integration enables individual electrical and optical addressing of active components on a single chip, allowing their concurrent operation while preserving coherent non-classical light emission. We demonstrate multiple quantum-photonic functionalities, including pure single-photon generation, two-photon interference, and resonant transmission and reflection measurements of integrated emitters. These results mark a step from isolated quantum-optical devices towards programmable quantum-photonic hardware platforms capable of combining coherent quantum emitters with large-scale photonic functionality.

item.title: Quantum Sensing Applications in Consumer Electronics: Emerging Methods and Near-Term Use Cases
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Near-term quantum sensing in consumer hardware is viable through hybrid upgrades rather than full replacements, with atomic vapor cells leading in maturity (160aT/Hz SERF magnetometry demonstrated) and navigation in GPS-denied environments offering the most practical initial entry point.

Grade 0.446 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Sounak Bhowmik, Himanshu Thapliyal

Figure

Integration workflow showing sensor initialization, coherent superposition preparation, signal interaction, and optical/electrical readout combined with classical post-processing in consumer hardware.

Asks

Where can quantum sensors deliver practical system-level advantages over conventional sensors when integrated into consumer electronics under real-world size, weight, power, and cost constraints?

But

Adoption limited by coherence times, optical alignment, thermal control, magnetic shielding overhead, and manufacturing packaging constraints for mass production.

Tools

nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond/SiC · atomic vapor cells · Rydberg atomic sensors · photonic quantum sensors · dynamical decoupling sequences

Abstract

Quantum sensing is emerging as a practical means of improving sensing capabilities in consumer electronics, particularly where size, power, and noise constrain classical approaches. In this paper, we reviewed the near-term applicability of quantum sensing using a platform-and-application framework. Within this framework, we outlined the general sensing protocol and discussed the working of the four key quantum sensing platforms relevant to consumer electronics: nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, atomic vapor cells, Rydberg atomic sensors, and photonic quantum sensors. Through case studies involving navigation and positioning, healthcare and wearables, radio-frequency (RF) and wireless systems, the Internet of Things (IoT), and imaging, we examined the tangible engineering advantages offered by quantum sensing. Rather than replacing devices outright, quantum sensing is more likely to earn its place in the near-term by upgrading specific measurement components within hybrid classical-quantum systems. Right now, the clearest opportunities are in weak-field detection, compact RF reception, and sensing that remains robust in noise.

item.title: Imaginary magnetic fields for ultracold atoms
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Four-level dissipative Raman scheme generates spatially uniform imaginary synthetic magnetic field 𝐁s=−isℏkRη𝐞z using position-dependent Raman coupling and state-dependent particle losses.

Grade 0.439 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Saulius Alminas, Domantas Burba, Gediminas Juzeliūnas

Figure

Trajectories and x-position center-of-mass evolution for Gaussian wavepackets launched in the synthetic imaginary magnetic field as functions of time and initial launch momentum ky0/kR.

Asks

How can a spatially uniform imaginary synthetic magnetic field be generated for ultracold atoms without closing the dressed-state gap or introducing unintended scalar loss gradients?

Before

Uniform imaginary vector potentials with zero curl were realized in Raman-coupled condensates (Tao et al. 2024), but linear detuning at fixed Raman amplitude gives non-uniform magnetic fields ∝(1−η2x2)−3/2 with gap closing.

But

Auxiliary state decay rates must exceed coherent couplings and motional energies (κλ≫ΩR,|ωλ|), dressed-state gap must remain much larger than non-adiabatic transitions, and |ηx|≪1 for quadratic vector potential approximation.

Tools

Four-level dissipative atom-light coupling · Adiabatic elimination / Schrieffer-Wolff transformation · Biorthogonal dressed states · Gaussian wavepacket dynamics

Abstract

We propose a four-level scheme for generating a uniform imaginary magnetic field for ultracold atoms using Raman coupling and state-dependent particle losses. Eliminating two lossy auxiliary states and subsequently projecting onto one of the two remaining Raman dressed atomic states, the atomic motion is affected by an imaginary vector potential with a constant curl corresponding to a spatially uniform imaginary synthetic magnetic field. We analytically derive the Gaussian wavepacket dynamics for atoms in such a synthetic magnetic field and study the width-dependent transport, which is unique to non-Hermitian systems. We find numerical agreement between the two-level non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and the adiabatic projection description, confirming the applicability of the latter adiabatic approach.

item.title: Decoy-state optical quantum information processing with coherent states
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Linear regression on phase-randomized coherent-state probes and threshold detectors predicts multi-photon Fock state interference statistics with absolute error on the order of 10−5 in the asymptotic limit and below 10−3 for total data sizes L=1011 to 1012. Estimates 4-photon and 6-photon interference using 32 and 256 probe settings, respectively.

Grade 0.429 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Wenyuan Wang, H. F. Chau

Figure

Average absolute error of predicted four-photon yield Y(1,1,1,1|1,1,1,1) plotted against total sent data size L. Shows error remains near 10−3 at L=1011–1012 signals, with Latin hypercube sampling outperforming full grid sampling at low data sizes.

Asks

How can multi-photon Fock state statistics and photon-number-resolving detection in optical circuits be accurately estimated using only phase-randomized coherent states and threshold detectors without linear programming instability?

Before

Numerical linear programming decoy-state post-processing (Ref. [12]) scaled only up to 3-photon inputs in a tritter and suffered severe numerical imprecision at higher photon numbers.

But

Numerical simulation. Highest accuracy relies on a unitary circuit prior with fixed Hilbert space dimensions; arbitrary non-unitary channels exhibit ill-conditioned scaling under finite-data statistical fluctuations.

Tools

phase-randomized coherent states · threshold detectors with variable attenuation · linear regression · Latin hypercube sampling

Abstract

Photonic qubits play an important role in quantum information processing. However, to date, efficient high-speed single photon sources and photon number resolving (PNR) detectors are still difficult to make. Here, we use phase-randomized coherent states and threshold detectors, combined with decoy-state post-processing, to simulate single photon sources and PNR detectors and perform various quantum information processing tasks. We propose a simple linear regression method to predict Fock state statistics based on observable statistics from coherent-state probes, combined with random/structured sampling of probe settings. Compared with traditional decoy-state post-processing based on linear programming and Cartesian product grid sampling, our method enables drastically improved accuracy and much reduced probe resources. It works particularly well for unknown unitary circuits of interest with fixed-size Hilbert space dimensions. For instance, it can accurately simulate 4-photon interference in linear optics with just 32 input/output probe settings and 6-photon interference with 256 probe settings. Moreover, it also works for non-unitary (such as lossy, nonlinear, or arbitrary) quantum channels. This enables a wide variety of applications that can be implemented with easily attainable coherent light sources and threshold detectors, such as characterization of small-scale linear optical quantum computing circuits or quantum sensing/metrology devices.

item.title: Arbitrary-phase CZ gate and remote readout across spatially separated superconducting nodes
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Realized deterministic arbitrary-phase CZ gate and single-shot readout across superconducting nodes separated by 30 m via bidirectional itinerant photon transfer, reaching maximum bidirectional transfer efficiency of 67%.

Grade 0.423 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Anatoly Kulikov, Josua D. Schär, Alonso Hernández-Antón, Aleksandr Grigorev

Figure

Reconstructed two-qubit density matrices for initial state |++⟩ across varying photon detunings δω=−5 MHz, 0, and 5 MHz, illustrating conditional phase tuning between nodes separated by 30 m.

Asks

Can a complete set of deterministic entangling operations and single-shot qubit readout be executed between spatially separated superconducting quantum nodes without active synchronization or classical communication?

Before

Unidirectional state transfer efficiency between nodes was 84.5% (Kurpiers 2018 / Magnard 2020).

But

Channel attenuation below 1 dB/km at < 60 mK; bidirectional efficiency constrained to 67% due to insertion losses across microwave adapters and connectors traversed twice.

Tools

30-m cryogenic superconducting waveguide link · frequency-tunable transmon qubits · time-reversed sideband Raman emission and absorption · dispersive cavity reflection phase shift

Abstract

Establishing a complete set of gates across spatially separated quantum nodes is fundamental for distributed quantum computation and communication networks. One of the approaches to do so consists of employing a superconducting device as a universal quantum node that is capable of storing and processing quantum information, and traveling microwave photons as means of communication. In this work, we realize an entangling gate across a primitive two-node superconducting circuit QED network consisting of two dilution cryostats, A and B, connected via a 30-m-long cryogenic quantum link. We perform a bidirectional photon transfer protocol, where a microwave photon emitted by the communication qubit at A acquires a conditional phase based on the state of qubit B. We vary the communication photon frequency, hence tuning the conditional phase acquired during the reflection off the remote node, effectively implementing an arbitrary-phase CZ gate. We use this entangling operation to perform single-shot readout of the qubit in node B from node A. An interesting feature of our scheme is that it does not require precise synchronization of the active node with the remote node; in particular, remote readout can be performed without any active participation by the remote node. These protocols add to the quantum communication toolbox with superconducting circuits and provide a way of realizing basic distributed quantum computing operations.

item.title: Beyond ideal cavities: quantifying the impact of cavity dissipation on light-matter strong coupling
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Cavity dissipation reduces the Rabi splitting of p-nitroaniline by more than 20% at realistic quality factors (Q=60) compared to the ideal lossless cavity limit, despite remaining in the strong-coupling regime.

Grade 0.422 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Giovanna Bruno, Enrico Busani, Lorenzo Gialli, Rosario Roberto Riso, Enrico Ronca

Figure

Polaritonic energy branches (eV) versus cavity resonance frequency (eV). Rabi splitting drops significantly when going from the ideal lossless limit (Q→∞) to a lossy cavity with Q=60 at τ=5.01 fs.

Asks

To what extent can finite cavity losses modify the energetics of strongly coupled light-matter systems when remaining within the strong-coupling regime?

But

Very weak damping approximation (1/Q2≪1), negligible mirror dispersion, linear field polarization, single-mode short-time Maclaurin expansion reference.

Tools

Dissipative Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian · QED-CCSD · Very weak damping approximation · eT program package

Abstract

Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (Cavity-QED) offers a powerful framework for controlling light-matter interactions, yet first-principles approaches commonly assume ideal, lossless cavity fields. Here, we introduce a minimal extension to the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian that accounts for cavity dissipation through the experimentally accessible cavity quality factor Q. The electromagnetic field is described as a damped harmonic oscillator within the very weak damping approximation. In this framework, cavity losses only enter the light-matter interaction and dipole self-energy terms, without introducing additional photonic degrees of freedom. A time-dependent unitary transformation yields a real-valued Hermitian Hamiltonian that can be incorporated into existing ab-initio QED methods without additional computational cost or changes in scaling. We combined the approach to the QED-CCSD method and investigated the effects of cavity dissipation on the optical spectrum of a p-nitroaniline molecule under strong light-matter coupling. We found that, for realistic quality factors, cavity dissipation can reduce the Rabi splitting by more than 20% compared to the ideal-cavity limit, even though the system remains in the strong-coupling regime. Convergence towards the ideal-cavity limit then requires substantially higher quality factors than those needed to establish strong coupling. These results demonstrate that cavity dissipation can significantly affect polaritonic energetics and highlight the importance of incorporating experimentally realistic cavity losses into quantitative ab-initio Cavity-QED simulations to accurately guide experimental protocols.

Can mid-circuit measurement and syndrome-extraction primitives be benchmarked across QPUs and code geometries using low-sampling algorithmic circuits without running full decoded QEC experiments?

Abstract

Quantum error correction (QEC) relies on repeated parity extraction, mid-circuit measurement (MCM), reset, feed-forward, and scheduling, yet these primitives are usually assessed either in isolation or through resource-demanding experiments. We introduce a few-sample benchmark of QEC-relevant primitives based on an MCM implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) with a fixed set of linear parameters (LR-QAOA). For a chosen code, the QAOA Hamiltonian is constructed from its check structure, such that the resulting circuit mimics the syndrome-extraction connectivity and MCM pattern while producing a direct algorithmic signal, the approximation-ratio r. The LR-QAOA depth, defined by the number of QAOA layers, plays a role analogous to the number of repeated syndrome-extraction rounds in a QEC experiment. From QPU executions, the decay of r with depth defines an effective hardware error, which we map to an equivalent two-qubit depolarizing rate λeff. We compare direct and MCM-mediated implementations across 10 QPUs from IBM, IQM, and Quantinuum, with circuits containing up to 2950 MCM operations. On Quantinuum's Helios-1 and H2-1, we run code-structured LR-QAOA benchmarks for surface-code, triangular color-code, and bivariate-bicycle qLDPC Hamiltonians up to 81, 91, and 48 data qubits, respectively, using up to 480 MCM operations. On IBM ibm_phoenix, we implement the surface-code structure and compare the LR-QAOA response with logical-memory experiments, observing a correlation between the benchmark and the logical performance across different regions of the QPU. Its construction and low resource requirements provide a practical benchmark for comparing hardware generations and QEC implementations before full logical-memory experiments are performed.

item.title: Polynomial neural surrogates for designing photonic quantum experiments
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Polynomial neural networks with single-layer activations matching perfect-matching edge counts σn/2(z)=zn/2 predict unnormalised photonic state amplitudes across n=4,6,8 photons, achieving validation loss 5.93×10−5 versus 2.85×10−1 for standard multilayer perceptrons at n=8 with 23-fold fewer parameters (5,535,256 vs 130,968,256). Inverse-design runtime for 8-photon linear-cluster states drops from 10349.96±7092.97 s via PyTheus to 15.25±14.35 s on GPU.

Grade 0.420 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Rohit Chaurasiya, Xuemei Gu

Figure

Initial (blue) and final (orange) fidelity distributions for 1000 independent inverse-design runs targeting GHZ, W, and linear-cluster states across n=4,6,8 photons using the PNN surrogate. All verified solutions achieve PyTheus fidelity F≥0.9999.

Asks

Can a physics-inspired neural surrogate accurately learn the polynomial graph-to-state mapping of a quantum-optics simulator and accelerate inverse experimental design?

Before

Direct optimization in PyTheus required 10349.96±7092.97 s for 8-photon linear-cluster inverse design on CPU; previous surrogates learned fixed target properties (like single-state fidelity) rather than full state amplitudes.

But

Restricted to 2 internal modes per photon, even photon counts n∈{4,6,8}, real-valued graph weights in [−1,1], and requires separate surrogate models trained for each photon number.

Tools

PyTheus simulator · Polynomial neural network (PNN) with z^(n/2) activations · Adam optimizer with cosine learning-rate decay · Jacobian sensitivity analysis

Code. https://github.com/AI-Quantum-Lab/PolySurrogate

Abstract

Physics simulators can support the discovery of quantum experiments by predicting the states generated by experimental configurations. When these simulators are computationally expensive, repeated simulator calls can limit the search for experiments that generate a desired quantum state. Here, we develop a physics-inspired polynomial neural surrogate for PyTheus, a graph-based quantum-optics simulator, to predict quantum states and use it to design quantum experiments. Its polynomial activations are motivated by the relation between graph perfect matchings and the resulting state amplitudes. We train separate surrogate models for four-, six-, and eight-photon systems and show that they achieve higher prediction accuracy with fewer trainable parameters than standard multilayer perceptrons. We then use the trained surrogates for inverse design of GHZ, W, and linear-cluster states. For the larger systems, the surrogates also enable faster inverse design than direct optimization with PyTheus. These results suggest that incorporating the underlying physics into neural surrogates can provide an efficient approach to quantum experiment design.
